html:
The oldest university in continuous operation, in Bologna, northern Italy. It dates its founding to 1088, a year chosen in the 1880s; the teaching of law there grew up in the late 1000s.

It began as a guild of students, many from abroad, who banded together to hire teachers and protect themselves from the townspeople. The Latin word universitas meant such a body. Students elected the rector and could fine lecturers who started late.

Bologna's fame came from law. Irnerius and his followers taught from the newly found Digest of Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis, and Gratian compiled church law there around 1140. Its lawyers served emperors, popes and cities across Europe.

The University of Paris and Oxford followed soon after, and the model spread across Europe. Older centres of higher learning existed elsewhere, such as Nalanda in India, al-Qarawiyyin in Fez and the University of Constantinople, but Bologna's self-governing body that grants degrees is the ancestor of the modern university. Copernicus studied there.
